Since the harmonic mean is always less than or equal to the arithmetic mean of the same two numbers, using the arithmetic-average formula for the transverse case always OVERSTATES the true transverse modulus -- exactly the error this KC's practice notes flag as the most common mistake.

exercises.prompt: In a continuous-fiber composite, why is the longitudinal modulus typically much higher than the transverse modulus?
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §16.10 style
options: Because the fibers carry a much larger share of the load when aligned with the loading direction (iso-strain, load-sharing proportional to stiffness), whereas transverse loading puts fiber and matrix in series (iso-stress), so the compliant matrix dominates
Because the fiber material itself changes properties depending on loading direction
Because transverse loading always causes immediate fracture
There is no real difference; this is a common misconception with no physical basis
exercises.explanation: Longitudinal (aligned) loading puts fiber and matrix in an iso-STRAIN configuration (parallel, like springs side by side) where the much stiffer fiber carries a disproportionate share of the load, pulling the effective composite modulus up close to the fiber's own high modulus. Transverse loading puts them in an iso-STRESS configuration (in series, like springs end to end) where the much more compliant matrix dominates the overall deformation, pulling the effective modulus down close to the matrix's much lower modulus -- hence the dramatic anisotropy. Option (b) incorrectly implies the fiber's intrinsic properties change; they don't -- only how the two phases share load changes with direction.

exercises.prompt: A boron fiber-aluminum matrix composite has Vf = 0.35, Ef = 400 GPa (boron), Em = 70 GPa (aluminum). Compute the longitudinal modulus Ec,L in GPa.
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §16.10 style

exercises.prompt: For the same boron fiber-aluminum matrix composite (Vf = 0.35, Ef = 400 GPa, Em = 70 GPa), compute the transverse modulus Ec,T using the inverse rule of mixtures, and state the ratio Ec,L/Ec,T (using Ec,L = 185.5 GPa from the previous problem) to quantify the composite's anisotropy.
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §16.10 style
exercises.solution: 1/Ec,T = Vf/Ef + (1-Vf)/Em = 0.35/400 + 0.65/70 = 0.000875 + 0.009286 = 0.010161 (1/GPa). Ec,T = 1/0.010161 approx 98.4 GPa. Anisotropy ratio: Ec,L/Ec,T = 185.5/98.4 approx 1.89 -- nearly a 2x difference between longitudinal and transverse stiffness for this fiber volume fraction, notably less extreme than a very high-Vf, high-fiber-modulus system (like the glass-epoxy example with a nearly 6x ratio) because boron's fiber modulus is 'only' about 5.7x the aluminum matrix modulus, compared to glass fiber's roughly 21x ratio over an epoxy matrix.

exercises.prompt: A Kevlar 49 fiber-epoxy composite has Vf = 0.45, Ef = 124 GPa, Em = 3.2 GPa. Compute both the longitudinal and transverse elastic modulus, setting up each formula yourself.
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §16.10 style
exercises.solution: Longitudinal: Ec,L = Vf*Ef + (1-Vf)*Em = 0.45(124) + 0.55(3.2) = 55.8 + 1.76 = 57.56 GPa. Transverse: 1/Ec,T = Vf/Ef + (1-Vf)/Em = 0.45/124 + 0.55/3.2 = 0.003629 + 0.171875 = 0.175504, so Ec,T = 1/0.175504 approx 5.70 GPa. The longitudinal-to-transverse ratio here is roughly 57.56/5.70 approx 10.1, a much larger anisotropy than the boron-aluminum case, driven by Kevlar's fiber modulus being nearly 39x the epoxy matrix's modulus (versus boron's roughly 5.7x over aluminum).

exercises.prompt: For a weight-critical, stiffness-limited design (e.g. an aircraft panel), why should a designer compare candidate materials using the INDEX E/rho (specific stiffness) rather than the absolute modulus E alone?
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §20.3 style
options: Because E/rho and E always rank materials identically, so it doesn't actually matter which is used
Because density is always more important than stiffness in any design

Because the design constraint is stiffness PER UNIT WEIGHT, and a material with lower absolute E but even lower density can achieve the same stiffness at less mass -- the raw E value alone ignores the weight side of the tradeoff entirely
Because absolute E values are impossible to measure accurately
exercises.explanation: When the actual constraint is 'achieve a given stiffness while minimizing weight' (or equivalently, 'maximize stiffness for a given weight'), the relevant merit index is specific stiffness E/rho, not E alone -- a material can have lower absolute modulus but be the better choice if its density is proportionally even lower, since less material mass is needed to achieve equivalent stiffness. Option (a) is false precisely in the classic aluminum-vs-steel comparison (aluminum has much lower E but comparable E/rho to steel). Options (d) and (b) are unrelated, unsupported claims.

exercises.prompt: On an Ashby materials-selection chart plotting two competing properties (e.g. strength vs. density), what does the absence of a single 'best' material at one point on the chart reflect?
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §20.3 style
options: That materials selection is essentially random and cannot be systematized

That real material selection is a multi-criteria tradeoff -- different materials occupy different points on the efficient tradeoff frontier, and which one is 'best' depends on how the specific design weighs the competing criteria
That only the material with the highest value of the y-axis property should ever be chosen
A flaw in how the chart was constructed
exercises.explanation: Ashby charts deliberately plot two (or more) competing properties precisely because real selection problems trade them off against each other -- the materials lying on the outer 'frontier' of the chart each represent a different, valid balance point between the two criteria, and which one is actually 'best' depends entirely on how a SPECIFIC application weighs those criteria (e.g. is weight or cost more critical here?). Options (a) and (c) both misread the tool: it doesn't imply randomness, and picking purely by one axis (d) throws away the entire point of plotting two properties at once.

exercises.prompt: Compare the specific stiffness (E/rho) of magnesium alloy (E = 45 GPa, rho = 1800 kg/m^3) against steel (E = 200 GPa, rho = 7850 kg/m^3). Compute magnesium's E/rho, in units of MN-m/kg (i.e., GPa/(kg/m^3) x 1000).
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §20.3 style
exercises.solution: E/rho for magnesium = 45e9 Pa / 1800 kg/m^3 = 2.5e7 m^2/s^2 = 25e6 (Pa*m^3/kg) = 25 MJ/kg (using consistent SI unit bookkeeping: Pa = N/m^2, so Pa/(kg/m^3) = N*m/kg = J/kg, and 25e6 J/kg = 25 MJ/kg = 25 MJ/kg). For comparison, steel's E/rho = 200e9/7850 = 2.548e7, essentially the SAME specific stiffness as magnesium (25.5 vs 25.0) despite magnesium's much lower absolute modulus -- illustrating why magnesium alloys remain competitive for stiffness-critical, weight-sensitive parts even though their absolute E is far below steel's.

exercises.prompt: Compare the specific strength (yield strength / density) of a titanium alloy (Sy = 880 MPa, rho = 4500 kg/m^3) against a carbon steel (Sy = 350 MPa, rho = 7850 kg/m^3). Compute both specific strengths and state which material would be favored for a weight-critical, strength-limited design (e.g. an aerospace strut), independent of cost considerations.
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §20.3 style
exercises.solution: Ti alloy: Sy/rho = 880e6/4500 = 1.956e5 J/kg (195.6 kJ/kg). Steel: Sy/rho = 350e6/7850 = 4.459e4 J/kg (44.6 kJ/kg). Titanium's specific strength is roughly 4.4x higher than the steel's -- for a purely weight-critical, strength-limited design (ignoring cost, which titanium alloys make far more expensive per unit mass), titanium would be strongly favored, needing far less mass to carry the same load. This is exactly why titanium alloys are used extensively in aerospace structures despite their high cost, while ordinary carbon steel remains preferred for cost-critical, less weight-sensitive applications.

exercises.prompt: In the thermal-shock-resistance parameter TSR = sigma_f*k/(E*alpha), which combination of property CHANGES would INCREASE a material's thermal shock resistance?
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §19.5 style
options: Any increase in modulus alone, regardless of the other three properties
TSR does not depend on thermal conductivity at all
Higher modulus and higher expansion coefficient, with lower strength and lower conductivity
Higher fracture strength and higher thermal conductivity, with lower modulus and lower expansion coefficient
exercises.explanation: TSR rewards properties in the numerator (strength sigma_f, conductivity k) and PENALIZES properties in the denominator (modulus E, expansion coefficient alpha) -- so higher strength and conductivity together with LOWER modulus and expansion coefficient all increase TSR. Option (c) has every term backwards. Option (a) ignores that E is in the denominator, so increasing it alone would actually DECREASE TSR, not increase it.

exercises.prompt: A ceramic coating with alpha_coating = 4e-6 /degC is applied to a metal substrate with alpha_metal = 12e-6 /degC. After a large temperature change, what is the most likely consequence at the coating-substrate interface?
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §19.3 style
options: No consequence, since coatings never experience internal stress from temperature changes
The coating will always expand more than the substrate, regardless of the alpha values given
Significant internal (thermal) stress develops at the interface because the two materials want to expand or contract by different amounts, which can crack or delaminate the coating
Thermal expansion mismatch only matters for polymers, not ceramic-metal systems
exercises.explanation: When two bonded materials with different expansion coefficients experience the same temperature change, they 'want' to change dimension by different amounts, but being bonded together forces them to deform together -- this generates internal stress at the interface (compressive or tensile depending on the sign of the temperature change and which material has the larger alpha), which is a common cause of coating cracking, spallation, or delamination in thermal-cycling service. Option (b) incorrectly asserts a fixed relationship regardless of the actual alpha values (here, the metal has the LARGER alpha, so it would expand MORE on heating, not the coating).

exercises.prompt: An aluminum panel is 3.0 m long at 20 degC. Aluminum's linear expansion coefficient is alpha = 23e-6 /degC. Find the change in length (in mm) when the panel reaches 60 degC.
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §19.3 style
exercises.solution: delta_T = 60 - 20 = 40 degC. delta_L = alpha*L0*delta_T = 23e-6 x 3.0 x 40 = 23e-6 x 120 = 2.76e-3 m = 2.76 mm.

exercises.prompt: Compute the thermal-shock-resistance parameter TSR = sigma_f*k/(E*alpha) for silicon nitride (sigma_f = 700 MPa, k = 25 W/m-K, E = 310 GPa, alpha = 3.2e-6 /degC) and for a typical firebrick refractory (sigma_f = 10 MPa, k = 1.0 W/m-K, E = 15 GPa, alpha = 5.5e-6 /degC). Which material better resists thermal shock, and by roughly what factor?
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §19.5 style
exercises.solution: Silicon nitride: TSR = (700e6 x 25)/(310e9 x 3.2e-6) = 1.75e10/9.92e5 approx 1.764e4 W/m. Firebrick: TSR = (10e6 x 1.0)/(15e9 x 5.5e-6) = 1.0e7/8.25e4 approx 121.2 W/m. Silicon nitride's TSR is roughly 1.764e4/121.2 approx 146x higher than firebrick's -- silicon nitride is dramatically better at resisting thermal shock, driven by its combination of much higher strength AND much higher thermal conductivity, despite also having a higher modulus (which alone would work against it). This is exactly why silicon nitride is used in applications with severe thermal cycling (e.g. turbocharger rotors, cutting tools) where firebrick-type refractories would crack.

exercises.prompt: A precision instrument requires a support structure that changes length by less than 0.01 mm over a 50 degC temperature swing, for a component length of 0.5 m. Compare ordinary steel (alpha = 12e-6 /degC) against Invar (a Fe-Ni alloy specifically engineered with alpha = 1.2e-6 /degC) for this application.
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §19.3 style
exercises.solution: Steel: delta_L = 12e-6 x 0.5 x 50 = 12e-6 x 25 = 3.0e-4 m = 0.30 mm -- far exceeds the 0.01 mm limit, making ordinary steel unsuitable. Invar: delta_L = 1.2e-6 x 0.5 x 50 = 1.2e-6 x 25 = 3.0e-5 m = 0.030 mm -- still exceeds 0.01 mm, though by a much smaller margin (10x better than steel). This illustrates why Invar (whose very low expansion coefficient comes from a specific magnetic/electronic compensation effect in its Fe-Ni composition) is specifically engineered and selected for precision instruments, clocks, and other applications where dimensional stability across temperature swings is critical, even though achieving the stated 0.01 mm tolerance here would still require either a shorter length, a smaller temperature swing, or an even lower-expansion material or active compensation.

exercises.prompt: In a galvanic couple between zinc and copper immersed in seawater, which metal corrodes, and why?
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §17.4 style
options: Neither corrodes when in contact; galvanic coupling always halts corrosion
Copper, because it is more chemically reactive
Both corrode at exactly the same rate
Zinc, because it is more anodic (higher on the active end of the galvanic series) than copper, so it preferentially gives up electrons
exercises.explanation: Zinc sits well above (more anodic/active than) copper on the galvanic series, meaning it more readily gives up electrons (oxidizes). When electrically coupled, the more anodic metal (zinc) becomes the sacrificial anode and corrodes preferentially, while the more noble/cathodic metal (copper) is protected -- this is the entire principle behind galvanizing steel and sacrificial anode protection systems. Option (a) is factually wrong; galvanic coupling typically ACCELERATES corrosion of the more anodic member, not halts it.

exercises.prompt: A metal's oxide has a Pilling-Bedworth ratio of 0.55. What does this predict about its oxide scale?
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §17.9 style
options: A porous, non-protective scale, since the oxide volume is substantially smaller than the metal volume it replaced, leaving gaps
A scale under such high compressive stress that it will definitely spall off in large flakes
PBR values below 1 are physically impossible
A well-protective, adherent scale, similar to aluminum's
exercises.explanation: A PBR well below 1 (like 0.55) means the oxide occupies LESS volume than the metal consumed to form it -- the oxide layer physically cannot fully cover the metal surface without gaps or porosity, so it provides little to no barrier against continued oxidation. Option (b) describes the opposite extreme (PBR >> 2, high compressive stress from oxide volume EXCEEDING metal volume). Option (c) is false; PBR < 1 is a real, well-documented case (e.g. alkali and alkaline-earth metals like sodium and magnesium).

exercises.prompt: Sodium oxidizes to Na2O. Molar mass of Na2O = 61.98 g/mol, density of Na2O = 2.27 g/cm^3. Molar mass of Na = 22.99 g/mol, density of Na = 0.97 g/cm^3. Each Na2O formula unit contains 2 Na atoms (n=2). Compute the Pilling-Bedworth ratio.
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §17.9 style
exercises.solution: PBR = (M_oxide x rho_metal)/(n x M_metal x rho_oxide) = (61.98 x 0.97)/(2 x 22.99 x 2.27) = 60.12/104.37 approx 0.576. This is well below 1, predicting (correctly) that sodium's oxide scale is non-protective and porous -- consistent with sodium's well-known reactivity and the need to store it under oil or inert atmosphere rather than relying on any passivating oxide layer.

exercises.prompt: Iron oxidizes to Fe2O3. Molar mass of Fe2O3 = 159.69 g/mol, density = 5.24 g/cm^3. Molar mass of Fe = 55.85 g/mol, density = 7.87 g/cm^3, n = 2 Fe atoms per Fe2O3 formula unit. Compute the PBR, classify the resulting scale, and explain why this matches iron's well-known tendency to rust progressively rather than passivate.
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §17.9 style
exercises.solution: PBR = (159.69 x 7.87)/(2 x 55.85 x 5.24) = 1,256.8/585.3 approx 2.147. Since PBR is well above 2, the growing oxide occupies substantially more volume than the metal consumed, putting the scale under high internal compressive stress -- this causes the scale to crack, buckle, and flake off (spall) rather than remaining as a continuous, adherent, protective layer. This is exactly why iron's rust does not passivate the surface the way aluminum's tightly-adherent Al2O3 (PBR approx 1.29) does: freshly exposed metal is continually revealed as the oxide spalls, allowing corrosion to proceed essentially unimpeded over time.

exercises.prompt: Explain, using the anode/cathode framework, why corrosion is fundamentally described as an ELECTROCHEMICAL process rather than a simple direct chemical reaction between a metal and its environment.
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §17.2-17.3 style
exercises.solution: Corrosion involves two spatially and functionally distinct half-reactions occurring simultaneously: an ANODIC reaction where the metal is oxidized (M -> M^n+ + n*e-, releasing electrons and metal ions into solution) and a CATHODIC reaction, typically elsewhere on the same surface or on a different metal in a galvanic couple, where those released electrons are consumed by a reduction reaction (commonly O2 + 2H2O + 4e- -> 4OH-, or 2H+ + 2e- -> H2 in acidic conditions). Because electrons must flow from the anodic site to the cathodic site (through the metal, acting as an electron conductor) and ions must flow through the electrolyte to complete the circuit, corrosion behaves like a tiny electrochemical cell (battery) rather than a simple one-step chemical reaction -- this framework is exactly what explains why galvanic coupling between dissimilar metals, or even localized composition/aeration differences on a single metal's surface, can dramatically accelerate or redirect corrosion.

exercises.prompt: Which characterization technique is used primarily to identify crystal structure and phase identity via characteristic diffraction peak positions?
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §3.16 style
options: X-ray diffraction (XRD)
Tensile testing
Vickers hardness testing
Optical microscopy
exercises.explanation: XRD reveals crystal structure and phase identity by measuring the characteristic angles (and hence interplanar spacings, via Bragg's law) at which a crystalline sample diffracts X-rays -- each phase and crystal structure produces a distinctive diffraction pattern. Optical microscopy (a) reveals grain size/microstructure at low-to-moderate magnification, not crystal structure. Hardness testing (c) and tensile testing (d) are mechanical property measurements, unrelated to crystal structure identification.

exercises.prompt: A researcher needs both high-resolution fracture-surface morphology AND the elemental composition of a small inclusion found on that fracture surface. Which single technique provides both in one measurement?
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §3.16 style
options: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with EDS (energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy)
X-ray diffraction alone
Tensile testing
Optical microscopy alone
exercises.explanation: SEM provides high-resolution imaging of surface morphology (far exceeding optical microscopy's resolution and depth of field, especially for rough fracture surfaces), and when paired with EDS, can also measure the elemental composition at a specific point or region the electron beam is focused on -- giving both morphology AND local composition in a single instrument session. Optical microscopy (a) lacks the resolution for fine fracture features and provides no elemental information. Tensile testing (c) and XRD alone (d) provide neither the morphology nor the localized elemental composition being asked for here.

exercises.prompt: A failure analysis team needs to determine: (1) the average grain size of a failed component, (2) whether a suspected phase transformation actually occurred (change in crystal structure), (3) the hardness profile across a case-hardened surface layer. Match each question to the appropriate technique.
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §3.16, §11.8 style
exercises.solution: (1) Optical microscopy (on a polished and etched cross-section) -- grain boundaries become visible under etching, and grain size can be measured directly or via a standard grain-size number method at low-to-moderate magnification. (2) X-ray diffraction (XRD) -- comparing diffraction patterns before and after suspected transformation directly reveals whether the crystal structure/phase has changed, since each phase has a distinct diffraction signature. (3) Vickers (or microhardness) testing at a series of points moving inward from the case-hardened surface -- a hardness PROFILE (not a single hardness number) requires multiple point measurements at increasing depth, which microhardness testing is specifically suited to provide.

exercises.prompt: Explain why a materials failure investigation typically uses MULTIPLE characterization techniques together rather than relying on just one, using a hypothetical brittle fracture investigation as the example.
exercises.source: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction 10e, §3.16 style
exercises.solution: Each technique reveals a fundamentally different aspect of the material, and a single failure mechanism typically leaves evidence across several of them simultaneously: SEM fractography would reveal the fracture SURFACE morphology (e.g. distinguishing a brittle cleavage fracture from a ductile dimpled fracture, or identifying a fatigue striation pattern), XRD could confirm whether an unexpected phase (e.g. untempered martensite) is present that would explain embrittlement, optical microscopy on a polished cross-section could reveal grain size or a heat-affected zone's microstructure, and hardness testing could map out whether the failure region shows anomalously high (brittle) or low (soft, overtempered) hardness relative to the surrounding material. Relying on only one of these would give an incomplete picture -- for instance, SEM alone might show a brittle fracture surface but couldn't confirm WHY the material was brittle (composition? phase? grain size? residual stress?), which is exactly the kind of question the other techniques are suited to answer.
